body:
🔬 The Cathode Ray Tube Experiment

In 1897, J.J. Thomson at Cambridge University was studying cathode rays — mysterious rays produced when high voltage was applied across a vacuum tube. These rays traveled from the cathode (negative electrode) to the anode (positive electrode). Thomson wanted to know: what are these rays made of?

He applied electric and magnetic fields to the rays and observed that they were deflected toward the positive plate and away from the negative plate. This proved the rays carried negative charge. He also found that the deflection was the same regardless of the gas used in the tube or the metal of the electrodes. This meant the particles were universal — they came from inside atoms.

⚖️ Measuring the Charge-to-Mass Ratio

Thomson then balanced the electric and magnetic forces on the cathode rays to measure their charge-to-mass ratio (e/m). He found:

  • e/m ≈ 1.76 × 10¹¹ coulombs per kilogram
  • This was about 1,800 times larger than the e/m of a hydrogen ion (the lightest known ion)

Thomson reasoned that either the particles had a huge charge or a tiny mass. Since the charge was not enormous, the particles must be extremely light. He called them electrons. This was the first discovery of a subatomic particle — proof that atoms are not indivisible.

🧪 The Plum Pudding Model

If atoms contain negatively charged electrons, but atoms are neutral overall, then there must be positive charge somewhere. Thomson proposed the Plum Pudding model: a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it like plums in a pudding. The electrons could vibrate within the positive sphere, explaining why heated atoms emit light of specific colors.

This model was a major advance — it was the first atomic model to include subatomic structure. But it had a problem: it could not explain the results of later experiments, especially Rutherford's gold foil experiment.

🛢️ Millikan's Oil Drop Experiment

In 1909, Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron directly. He sprayed tiny oil droplets between two electrically charged plates. By adjusting the voltage, he could make a charged droplet hover motionless — the electric force balanced the gravitational force. From this, he calculated the charge on each droplet.

Millikan found that all charges were integer multiples of a fundamental value: 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. This is the elementary charge. Combined with Thomson's e/m ratio, Millikan's result allowed scientists to calculate the electron's mass: 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

🧪 Worked Example: Calculating Electron Mass

Question: Thomson measured e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg. Millikan measured e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the mass of the electron.

Solution:

  • e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg
  • m = e / (e/m)
  • m = (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) / (1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg)
  • m ≈ 9.10 × 10⁻³¹ kg

This is the rest mass of the electron — about 1/1836 the mass of a proton.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • CRT televisions and monitors — Older TVs used cathode ray tubes to produce images by steering electron beams onto a phosphorescent screen.
  • Electron microscopes — Use electron beams instead of light to achieve much higher magnification.
  • X-ray tubes — Electrons striking a metal target produce X-rays used in medical imaging.
  • Semiconductors — Understanding electron behavior is essential for designing transistors and computer chips.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Thomson discovered the proton.' Reality: Thomson discovered the electron. The proton was discovered later by Rutherford (1917).
  • Misconception: 'The Plum Pudding model was completely wrong.' Reality: It was the first model with subatomic structure — a crucial step, even though it was later replaced.
  • Misconception: 'Electrons are the only subatomic particles.' Reality: Atoms also contain protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a glass tube with a cathode (negative electrode) at one end and an anode (positive electrode) at the other. A beam of cathode rays travels from cathode to anode. Two charged plates create an electric field perpendicular to the beam. The beam bends toward the positive plate, showing the rays are negatively charged. A fluorescent screen at the far end shows a glowing spot where the beam hits.

2.intro: In 1909, Ernest Rutherford and his team performed one of the most famous experiments in physics: the gold foil experiment. The results were so surprising that Rutherford said it was 'almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.' This lesson explores how the gold foil experiment revealed the atomic nucleus and led to the nuclear model of the atom. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIb-9.

body:
🔬 The Setup of the Gold Foil Experiment

Ernest Rutherford, working at the University of Manchester with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, designed an experiment to test Thomson's Plum Pudding model. They fired a beam of alpha particles (positively charged, relatively heavy) at a very thin sheet of gold foil (only a few atoms thick).

Around the foil, they placed a fluorescent screen (zinc sulfide) that would light up when hit by an alpha particle. By observing where the flashes appeared, they could determine how the alpha particles were deflected.

📊 Expected Results

According to Thomson's Plum Pudding model, the positive charge is spread throughout the atom. Alpha particles are much more massive than electrons and carry a lot of momentum. If the positive charge were spread out, the alpha particles should pass through the foil with only tiny deflections — maybe 1 or 2 degrees at most. Most should go straight through.

😲 Actual Results

What actually happened was astonishing:

  • Most alpha particles (about 99%) passed straight through the foil with little or no deflection.
  • Some (about 1%) were deflected by large angles — more than 90 degrees.
  • A few (about 1 in 8,000) bounced straight back toward the source.

Rutherford later described this as 'almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.'

🧠 What the Results Meant

Rutherford reasoned:

  • If most alpha particles pass straight through, the atom is mostly empty space.
  • If some are deflected by large angles, they must be hitting something massive and positively charged.
  • If a few bounce straight back, that massive positive charge must be concentrated in a very tiny volume.

He concluded that the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its center. The electrons orbit around this nucleus. Most of the atom's volume is empty space.

📐 Size Comparison

If the nucleus were the size of a marble (about 1 cm), the atom would be about 1 kilometer in diameter. The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller than the atom. Yet it contains more than 99.9% of the atom's mass.

🧪 Worked Example: Estimating Nuclear Size

Question: If an alpha particle is deflected by 180 degrees (bounces straight back), what does that tell you about the nucleus?

Solution:

  • A 180-degree deflection means the alpha particle's momentum was reversed.
  • This requires a very strong electrostatic repulsive force from a massive, positively charged object.
  • For the alpha particle to be repelled without penetrating, the nucleus must be extremely dense and tiny.
  • This led Rutherford to estimate the nuclear radius is about 10⁻¹⁵ m, compared to the atomic radius of about 10⁻¹⁰ m.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Nuclear power — Understanding the nucleus is essential for nuclear fission and fusion energy.
  • Medical imaging — PET scans use positron emission from nuclear decay.
  • Radiocarbon dating — Uses nuclear decay of carbon-14 to date ancient objects.
  • Particle accelerators — Like the Large Hadron Collider, they probe nuclear and subatomic structure.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Electrons orbit the nucleus like planets orbit the Sun.' Reality: Electrons do not follow definite paths. They exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
  • Misconception: 'The nucleus is large.' Reality: The nucleus is tiny — about 1/100,000 of the atom's diameter.
  • Misconception: 'Rutherford discovered the nucleus.' Reality: He discovered the nucleus, but the proton was identified later by Rutherford (1917) and confirmed by others.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a beam of alpha particles (helium nuclei) fired at a thin gold foil. Most pass straight through, shown as straight lines. A few are deflected at small angles, shown as slightly bent lines. A very few are deflected at large angles or bounce straight back, shown as sharply bent or reversed lines. Around the foil is a circular fluorescent screen that lights up where particles hit.

3.intro: Rutherford's nuclear model left a major problem: according to classical physics, electrons orbiting a nucleus should lose energy and spiral inward, causing the atom to collapse. Yet atoms are stable. In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a revolutionary solution: electrons can only exist in specific energy levels. This lesson explores Moseley's contribution to atomic number and Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIb-10.

The lowest energy state of an electron in an atom.
A higher energy state of an electron, achieved by absorbing energy.
A quantum of light energy — emitted or absorbed when an electron transitions between energy levels.

body:
🔢 Moseley and Atomic Number

In 1913, Henry Moseley used X-ray spectroscopy to determine the atomic number (Z) of elements. He found that the frequency of X-rays emitted by an element depends on the number of protons in its nucleus — not on its atomic mass. This was a crucial discovery: it established that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the fundamental property that defines an element.

Moseley's work reorganized the periodic table. Some elements that had been placed by atomic mass were now correctly ordered by atomic number. For example, cobalt (Z=27) and nickel (Z=28) were swapped. Moseley's law: √f ∝ (Z - 1).

⚠️ The Problem with Rutherford's Model

Rutherford's model had a fatal flaw. According to classical electromagnetism, an electron orbiting a nucleus is constantly accelerating (changing direction). Accelerating charges emit electromagnetic radiation, losing energy. The electron should spiral into the nucleus in about 10⁻¹¹ seconds. But atoms are stable — they don't collapse. Something was missing.

💡 Bohr's Postulates

Niels Bohr proposed three revolutionary postulates:

  • Quantized orbits — Electrons can only occupy specific, discrete energy levels. They cannot exist between these levels.
  • No radiation in stable orbits — Electrons in allowed orbits do not emit energy, even though they are accelerating. This violated classical physics but explained stability.
  • Energy transitions — Electrons emit or absorb a photon only when they jump between energy levels. The photon energy equals the energy difference: ΔE = hf.

📊 The Hydrogen Emission Spectrum

When hydrogen gas is excited (by heat or electricity), it emits light at specific wavelengths — not a continuous rainbow. This is the emission spectrum. Bohr's model explained it perfectly:

  • Electron absorbs energy and jumps to a higher level (excited state).
  • Electron falls back to a lower level, emitting a photon with energy equal to the difference.
  • The wavelength of the photon determines the color of light.

The visible hydrogen lines are called the Balmer series. The Lyman series is in the ultraviolet. The Paschen series is in the infrared.

🧮 Worked Example: Energy of an Electron Transition

Question: An electron in a hydrogen atom drops from n=3 to n=2. Calculate the energy and wavelength of the emitted photon.

Solution:

  • Energy of level n: Eₙ = -13.6 eV / n²
  • E₃ = -13.6 / 9 = -1.51 eV
  • E₂ = -13.6 / 4 = -3.40 eV
  • ΔE = E₃ - E₂ = -1.51 - (-3.40) = 1.89 eV
  • Convert to joules: 1.89 eV × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/eV = 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
  • Using E = hc/λ: λ = hc / E
  • λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)(3.00 × 10⁸ m/s) / (3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
  • λ ≈ 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m = 656 nm (red light)

This is the famous H-alpha line — the red line in hydrogen's emission spectrum.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Neon signs — Different gases emit different colors due to their unique energy levels.
  • Astronomy — Emission spectra identify elements in stars and galaxies.
  • Lasers — Operate on the principle of electron transitions between quantized energy levels.
  • LEDs — Light-emitting diodes use electron transitions in semiconductor materials.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Bohr's model is completely correct.' Reality: Bohr's model works well for hydrogen but fails for multi-electron atoms. Quantum mechanics replaced it.
  • Misconception: 'Electrons orbit like planets.' Reality: In Bohr's model, orbits are quantized, but in modern quantum mechanics, electrons exist in probability clouds.
  • Misconception: 'Atomic number is the same as atomic mass.' Reality: Atomic number is the number of protons; atomic mass is the total mass of protons, neutrons, and electrons.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a series of concentric circles around a central nucleus. The innermost circle is n=1 (ground state), then n=2, n=3, etc. An electron absorbs energy and jumps from n=2 to n=3 (excited state). When it falls back to n=2, a photon is emitted. The energy of the photon equals the energy difference between the two levels.

4.intro: Bohr's model was a triumph for hydrogen, but it failed for atoms with more than one electron. The solution came from quantum mechanics — a radical new physics that described electrons as waves, not particles. This lesson explores the quantum mechanical model of the atom, the concept of orbitals, and how this model explains the periodic table. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIb-10 (continuation).

body:
⚠️ Limitations of Bohr's Model

Bohr's model worked beautifully for hydrogen but failed for helium and heavier atoms. It could not explain:

  • Why multi-electron atoms have more complex spectra
  • Why some spectral lines split in magnetic fields (Zeeman effect)
  • Why electrons in the same orbit repel each other
  • The chemical behavior of elements beyond hydrogen

A new model was needed — one based on quantum mechanics.

🌊 Wave-Particle Duality

In 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed that particles like electrons have wave-like properties. The wavelength of a particle is λ = h / mv, where h is Planck's constant, m is mass, and v is velocity. This was confirmed experimentally: electrons can diffract and interfere like waves.

Erwin Schrödinger developed a wave equation that describes the electron as a standing wave around the nucleus. The solutions to this equation give the probability of finding the electron at any point in space.

☁️ Orbitals, Not Orbits

In the quantum mechanical model, electrons do not travel in definite paths (orbits). Instead, they exist in orbitals — regions of space where the electron is likely to be found. An orbital is a probability cloud, not a trajectory.

Each orbital is described by four quantum numbers:

  • n — principal quantum number (shell): 1, 2, 3, ...
  • l — angular momentum quantum number (subshell): s, p, d, f
  • mₗ — magnetic quantum number (orientation in space)
  • mₛ — spin quantum number: +½ or -½

📊 Orbital Shapes

Orbitals have characteristic shapes:

  • s orbitals — spherical
  • p orbitals — dumbbell-shaped, three orientations (px, py, pz)
  • d orbitals — clover-shaped, five orientations
  • f orbitals — complex shapes, seven orientations

These shapes determine how atoms bond and interact.

🔢 Electron Configuration and the Periodic Table

Electrons fill orbitals according to the Aufbau principle (lowest energy first) and the Pauli exclusion principle (max two electrons per orbital, opposite spins). The electron configuration explains the structure of the periodic table:

  • Group 1 (alkali metals) — ns¹ configuration
  • Group 17 (halogens) — ns² np⁵ configuration
  • Group 18 (noble gases) — full outer shells (ns² np⁶)

Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence electrons.

🧮 Worked Example: Electron Configuration of Oxygen (Z=8)

Question: Write the electron configuration of oxygen.

Solution:

  • Oxygen has 8 electrons.
  • Fill lowest energy orbitals first: 1s (2 electrons), 2s (2 electrons), 2p (4 electrons).
  • Configuration: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴
  • Valence electrons: 6 (2s² 2p⁴)
  • Oxygen is in Group 16 (chalcogens) and Period 2.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Chemistry — Orbital shapes explain molecular geometry and bonding.
  • Materials science — Semiconductor behavior depends on electron configuration.
  • Spectroscopy — Quantum mechanics explains atomic and molecular spectra.
  • Periodic table — The organization of elements is a direct consequence of electron configuration.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Orbitals are the same as orbits.' Reality: Orbits are definite paths (Bohr); orbitals are probability clouds (quantum mechanics).
  • Misconception: 'Electrons are tiny balls.' Reality: Electrons exhibit wave-particle duality and are best described by wave functions.
  • Misconception: 'The Bohr model is still the best model.' Reality: Bohr's model is a useful stepping stone, but quantum mechanics is more accurate.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a central nucleus surrounded by fuzzy clouds. The s orbital is a sphere around the nucleus. The p orbitals are three dumbbell shapes oriented along the x, y, and z axes. The d orbitals are five clover-leaf shapes. These clouds represent where the electron is likely to be found — denser regions mean higher probability.

1.intro: By the early 20th century, scientists understood that atoms have a nucleus containing protons and neutrons. But they soon discovered that nuclei are not always stable — some spontaneously change into other elements, releasing energy in the process. This lesson explores atomic number, isotopes, and the phenomenon of nuclear transmutation: the conversion of one element into another. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIb-11.

Explain how the discovery of transmutation fulfilled the ancient alchemists' quest

body:
🔢 Atomic Number and Mass Number

The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in an atom's nucleus. It is the single most important number for identifying an element — no two elements have the same atomic number. The mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons. The number of neutrons is therefore N = A - Z.

Notation: ᴬ_Z X, where X is the element symbol, A is the mass number (superscript), and Z is the atomic number (subscript). For example, ¹²₆C is carbon-12: 6 protons and 6 neutrons.

⚖️ Isotopes: Same Element, Different Mass

Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons. For example:

  • Carbon-12: 6 protons, 6 neutrons (stable)
  • Carbon-13: 6 protons, 7 neutrons (stable)
  • Carbon-14: 6 protons, 8 neutrons (radioactive)

Because isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons, they have identical chemical properties. Their physical properties (mass, density, rate of diffusion) differ slightly.

⚗️ Nuclear Transmutation: The Alchemist's Dream

For centuries, alchemists tried to turn lead into gold — without success. In 1919, Ernest Rutherford achieved the first artificial nuclear transmutation: he bombarded nitrogen atoms with alpha particles, producing oxygen and a proton.

Equation: ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + ¹₁H

This was a historic moment — humans had changed one element into another. In 1932, Cockcroft and Walton transmuted lithium into helium using accelerated protons. Today, transmutation is routine in nuclear reactors and particle accelerators.

🧮 Balancing Nuclear Equations

In any nuclear reaction, two conservation laws must hold:

  • Conservation of mass number (A) — sum of A on the left = sum of A on the right
  • Conservation of atomic number (Z) — sum of Z on the left = sum of Z on the right

These rules allow you to predict unknown products or reactants.

🧪 Worked Example: Balancing a Transmutation Equation

Question: Complete the equation: ²⁷₁₃Al + ⁴₂He → ? + ¹₀n

Solution:

  • Mass number: 27 + 4 = 31 on the left. On the right, 1 (neutron) + ? = 31, so ? = 30.
  • Atomic number: 13 + 2 = 15 on the left. On the right, 0 (neutron) + ? = 15, so ? = 15.
  • Element with Z=15 is phosphorus (P).
  • Answer: ³⁰₁₅P (phosphorus-30)

This is the reaction used by Irène and Frédéric Joliot-Curie in 1934 to create the first artificial radioactive isotope.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Nuclear medicine — Radioactive isotopes like technetium-99m are used for imaging.
  • Radiocarbon dating — Carbon-14 transmutation in the atmosphere allows dating of ancient artifacts.
  • Nuclear power — Transmutation of uranium produces energy and plutonium.
  • Particle accelerators — Create new elements by transmutation (e.g., oganesson, Z=118).

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Transmutation is impossible.' Reality: It occurs naturally in radioactive decay and is routinely achieved in laboratories.
  • Misconception: 'Isotopes have different chemical properties.' Reality: Isotopes of the same element have identical chemical properties because they have the same electron configuration.
  • Misconception: 'Mass number is the same as atomic mass.' Reality: Mass number is an integer (protons + neutrons); atomic mass is a weighted average of isotope masses (not an integer).

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a nitrogen nucleus (7 protons, 7 neutrons) being struck by an alpha particle (2 protons, 2 neutrons). The collision produces an oxygen nucleus (8 protons, 9 neutrons) and a proton (1 proton, 0 neutrons). The total number of protons and neutrons is conserved before and after the reaction.

2.intro: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and spontaneously emit particles or radiation to become more stable. This process is called radioactive decay. In this lesson, we explore the three main types of radioactive decay — alpha, beta, and gamma — and how they change the nucleus. We also examine the concept of half-life and how it is used to date materials and diagnose diseases. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIb-12.

vocabulary.definition: The spontaneous emission of particles or radiation from unstable atomic nuclei.
Emission of an alpha particle (⁴₂He) from a nucleus, decreasing the mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2.
Emission of a beta particle (⁰₋₁e) when a neutron converts into a proton, increasing the atomic number by 1.
Emission of high-energy gamma radiation (⁰₀γ) as a nucleus transitions from an excited state to a lower energy state — no change in mass or atomic number.
The time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
The ability of radiation to pass through matter — alpha < beta < gamma.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, potentially damaging biological molecules.
Determining the age of a material by measuring the ratio of radioactive isotopes to their decay products.

body:
☢️ What Is Radioactive Decay?

Not all nuclei are stable. Some have too many protons, too many neutrons, or too much energy. To become more stable, they spontaneously emit particles or radiation. This process is radioactive decay. It is random at the level of individual nuclei but predictable for large samples.

🔴 Alpha Decay

In alpha decay, a nucleus emits an alpha particle (⁴₂He), which consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons. The parent nucleus loses 4 mass units and 2 atomic number units.

Example: ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He

Alpha particles have low penetrating power (stopped by paper or skin) but are highly ionizing and dangerous if inhaled or ingested.

🔵 Beta Decay

In beta decay, a neutron converts into a proton and emits a beta particle (⁰₋₁e, an electron) and an antineutrino. The mass number stays the same, but the atomic number increases by 1.

Example: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e

Beta particles are more penetrating than alpha particles (stopped by a few millimeters of aluminum) but less ionizing.

🟡 Gamma Decay

In gamma decay, an excited nucleus releases excess energy as a gamma ray (⁰₀γ). The mass number and atomic number remain unchanged — the nucleus simply moves to a lower energy state.

Example: ⁹⁹ᵐ₄₃Tc → ⁹⁹₄₃Tc + ⁰₀γ

Gamma rays are highly penetrating (require thick lead or concrete to stop) but are less ionizing than alpha particles.

⏳ Half-Life

The half-life (t₁/₂) is the time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. After one half-life, 50% remains. After two half-lives, 25% remains. After n half-lives, the remaining fraction is (1/2)ⁿ.

Half-lives range from fractions of a second (e.g., francium-223: 22 minutes) to billions of years (e.g., uranium-238: 4.5 billion years).

🧮 Worked Example: Half-Life Calculation

Question: A sample of iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. If you start with 80 mg, how much remains after 32 days?

Solution:

  • Number of half-lives: 32 days / 8 days = 4 half-lives
  • Remaining fraction: (1/2)⁴ = 1/16
  • Remaining mass: 80 mg × 1/16 = 5 mg

After 32 days, 5 mg of iodine-131 remains.

🧪 Worked Example: Balancing a Beta Decay Equation

Question: Complete: ³²₁₅P → ? + ⁰₋₁e

Solution:

  • Mass number: 32 = ? + 0, so ? = 32
  • Atomic number: 15 = ? + (-1), so ? = 16
  • Element with Z=16 is sulfur (S).
  • Answer: ³²₁₆S

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Medical imaging — Technetium-99m (gamma emitter) used in bone scans and heart imaging.
  • Cancer treatment — Cobalt-60 and radium-226 used in radiotherapy.
  • Radiocarbon dating — Carbon-14 (half-life 5,730 years) dates organic remains up to ~50,000 years.
  • Nuclear power — Uranium-235 and plutonium-239 undergo fission in reactors.
  • Smoke detectors — Americium-241 (alpha emitter) ionizes air to detect smoke.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Radioactive materials glow green.' Reality: Most radioactivity is invisible. Glowing is a chemical effect, not nuclear.
  • Misconception: 'All radiation is dangerous.' Reality: We are constantly exposed to background radiation. Risk depends on dose, type, and exposure time.
  • Misconception: 'Half-life means half the sample disappears.' Reality: Half the radioactive nuclei decay, but the total mass changes only slightly (decay products remain).

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine three types of radiation passing through barriers. Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper. Beta particles pass through paper but are stopped by a few millimeters of aluminum. Gamma rays pass through paper and aluminum but are stopped by thick lead or concrete. The diagram shows the relative penetrating power of each type.

3.intro: Radioactive decay occurs naturally, but in the 1930s scientists discovered how to induce nuclear reactions artificially. This led to the discovery of the neutron, the creation of new elements, and ultimately the development of nuclear fission and nuclear power. This lesson explores artificial transmutation, the discovery of the neutron, and the beginnings of the nuclear age. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIb-12 (continuation).
objectives: Describe James Chadwick's discovery of the neutron and its importance
Explain how artificial transmutation is achieved using particle accelerators
Describe the discovery of nuclear fission and the role of neutrons in chain reactions
Explain the difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion

vocabulary.definition: A neutral subatomic particle found in the nucleus, with a mass slightly larger than a proton.
The conversion of one element into another by bombarding nuclei with particles.
A machine that accelerates charged particles to high speeds for collision experiments.
The splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons.
The combining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
A self-sustaining nuclear reaction in which neutrons released by fission trigger further fissions.
The minimum amount of fissile material needed to sustain a nuclear chain reaction.
A radioactive isotope, often produced artificially for medical or industrial use.

body:
🔍 The Discovery of the Neutron

By 1930, scientists knew atoms contained protons and electrons. But the mass of atoms didn't add up — helium had 2 protons but a mass of 4. Where was the extra mass? In 1932, James Chadwick solved the puzzle by discovering the neutron — a neutral particle with a mass similar to a proton. The neutron was found in the nucleus, explaining the missing mass and the existence of isotopes.

⚡ Artificial Transmutation

Rutherford's 1919 experiment showed that alpha particles could transmute nitrogen into oxygen. But alpha particles are relatively heavy and slow. To achieve more transmutations, scientists needed higher-energy particles. Particle accelerators were developed in the 1930s to accelerate protons, deuterons, and other particles to high speeds, smashing them into target nuclei.

In 1932, John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton built the first particle accelerator and transmuted lithium into helium: ⁷₃Li + ¹₁H → 2 ⁴₂He. This was the first nuclear reaction powered entirely by human-made technology.

💥 Nuclear Fission

In 1938, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced much lighter elements — barium and krypton. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained this as nuclear fission: the uranium nucleus had split into two smaller nuclei, releasing enormous energy and several neutrons.

Equation: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n + energy

The released neutrons can trigger further fissions, creating a chain reaction. This is the basis of nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons.

⚛️ Nuclear Fusion

Nuclear fusion is the opposite of fission: light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy. Fusion powers the Sun and stars.

Equation: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + energy

Fusion releases more energy per gram than fission but requires extremely high temperatures and pressures to overcome electrostatic repulsion. Controlled fusion is a major research goal (ITER, NIF).

🧮 Worked Example: Energy from Fission

Question: In the fission of one uranium-235 nucleus, about 200 MeV of energy is released. How much energy is released by the fission of 1 gram of U-235?

Solution:

  • Number of U-235 atoms in 1 g: (1 g) / (235 g/mol) × 6.022 × 10²³ atoms/mol ≈ 2.56 × 10²¹ atoms
  • Energy = 2.56 × 10²¹ × 200 MeV = 5.12 × 10²³ MeV
  • Convert to joules: 1 MeV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹³ J
  • Energy ≈ 5.12 × 10²³ × 1.602 × 10⁻¹³ J ≈ 8.2 × 10¹⁰ J

This is equivalent to the energy from burning about 2,500 tons of coal.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Nuclear power plants — Use controlled fission of U-235 to generate electricity.
  • Nuclear weapons — Use uncontrolled chain reactions (atomic bombs: fission; hydrogen bombs: fusion).
  • Medical isotopes — Produced in reactors and cyclotrons for diagnosis and therapy.
  • Space exploration — Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) power deep-space probes.
  • Fusion research — ITER aims to demonstrate controlled fusion as a clean energy source.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Nuclear reactors can explode like atomic bombs.' Reality: Reactor fuel is not enriched enough for a nuclear explosion. Reactor accidents (Chernobyl, Fukushima) involve steam explosions and meltdowns, not nuclear detonations.
  • Misconception: 'Fission and fusion are the same.' Reality: Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion combines light nuclei. Both release energy but by different mechanisms.
  • Misconception: 'Nuclear energy is completely clean.' Reality: It produces no greenhouse gases but creates radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a uranium-235 nucleus absorbing a neutron, becoming unstable, and splitting into two smaller nuclei (barium and krypton) plus three neutrons. The released neutrons strike other uranium nuclei, causing more fissions — a chain reaction. The diagram shows the branching pattern of increasing fissions.

4.intro: Radioactive decay and nuclear reactions have profound effects on the environment, human health, and society. This lesson examines the biological effects of radiation, the challenges of nuclear waste, and the role of nuclear technology in medicine and energy. We also explore the ethical and environmental dimensions of living in the nuclear age. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIb-12 (continuation).

Explain the difference between acute and chronic radiation exposure
Describe how nuclear waste is classified and managed

vocabulary.definition: Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, damaging biological molecules.
The SI unit of radiation dose, measuring the biological effect of radiation.
A large dose of radiation received in a short time, causing immediate effects like radiation sickness.
Small doses of radiation received over a long period, increasing long-term cancer risk.
Materials containing radioactive isotopes that must be stored safely until they decay to safe levels.
As Low As Reasonably Achievable — the principle of minimizing radiation exposure.
The use of ionizing radiation to treat cancer by damaging cancer cell DNA.

body:
🧬 Biological Effects of Radiation

Ionizing radiation can damage biological molecules, especially DNA. When radiation strikes a cell, it can:

  • Break DNA strands — leading to mutations or cell death.
  • Create free radicals — reactive molecules that damage proteins and lipids.
  • Cause cell death — high doses kill cells directly, causing tissue damage.

Cells can repair some damage, but unrepaired DNA damage can lead to cancer. Rapidly dividing cells (bone marrow, gut lining, reproductive cells) are most sensitive to radiation.

📊 Dose and Risk

Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv). Typical doses:

  • Background radiation: ~2–3 mSv/year
  • Dental X-ray: ~0.005 mSv
  • Chest CT scan: ~7 mSv
  • Occupational limit: 50 mSv/year
  • Acute radiation sickness: >1 Sv
  • Lethal dose: ~4–5 Sv without treatment

Risk increases with dose, but even low doses carry some risk. The linear no-threshold model assumes risk is proportional to dose, even at low levels.

⚠️ Acute vs. Chronic Exposure

Acute exposure — a large dose in a short time (e.g., nuclear accident) causes immediate effects: nausea, burns, hair loss, organ failure. Chronic exposure — small doses over years (e.g., radon in homes) increases long-term cancer risk without immediate symptoms.

🗑️ Nuclear Waste Management

Nuclear reactors produce radioactive waste, classified by activity level:

  • Low-level waste — contaminated clothing, tools, filters. Stored in shallow trenches.
  • Intermediate-level waste — reactor components, chemical sludge. Encased in concrete or bitumen.
  • High-level waste — spent fuel rods. Highly radioactive, requires deep geological storage for thousands of years.

Finland's Onkalo repository is the world's first permanent deep geological disposal site, designed to store waste for 100,000 years.

⚖️ Nuclear Power: Benefits and Risks

Benefits:

  • Low greenhouse gas emissions
  • High energy density — 1 kg of uranium yields energy equivalent to 2,500 tons of coal
  • Reliable baseload power

Risks:

  • Radioactive waste storage
  • Accident potential (Chernobyl, Fukushima)
  • Nuclear proliferation (weapons)
  • High upfront costs

🏥 Radiation in Medicine

Radiation is used in:

  • Diagnosis — X-rays, CT scans, PET scans, bone scans.
  • Therapy — Radiotherapy kills cancer cells using targeted radiation.
  • Sterilization — Gamma rays sterilize medical equipment.

The ALARA principle guides medical use: minimize dose while achieving diagnostic or therapeutic goals.

🧮 Worked Example: Comparing Radiation Doses

Question: A patient receives a chest CT scan (7 mSv) and a dental X-ray (0.005 mSv). How many dental X-rays equal one CT scan?

Solution:

  • 7 mSv / 0.005 mSv = 1,400
  • One CT scan = 1,400 dental X-rays

This illustrates why CT scans are used only when medically necessary — the dose is much higher than simpler imaging.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Radon testing — Radon gas in homes is a leading cause of lung cancer among non-smokers.
  • Nuclear accidents — Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011) shaped public perception of nuclear risk.
  • Medical physics — Radiation therapists and physicists ensure safe and effective treatment.
  • Space travel — Astronauts face higher radiation exposure beyond Earth's magnetic field.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Any radiation is deadly.' Reality: We are exposed to background radiation daily. Risk depends on dose and type.
  • Misconception: 'Nuclear waste can be made safe instantly.' Reality: High-level waste remains radioactive for thousands of years and requires long-term storage.
  • Misconception: 'Radiation only comes from nuclear plants.' Reality: Natural sources (radon, cosmic rays, potassium-40 in food) contribute most background radiation.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a graph showing radiation dose on the x-axis (log scale) and biological effect on the y-axis. Low doses (<100 mSv) show no immediate effects. Moderate doses (100 mSv–1 Sv) increase cancer risk. High doses (>1 Sv) cause acute radiation sickness. Very high doses (>5 Sv) are lethal. The graph illustrates the dose-response relationship.

1.intro: Atoms rarely exist alone — they bond together to form molecules and compounds. The way atoms bond determines everything about a substance: its shape, its melting point, its solubility, and even its biological function. This lesson explores the nature of chemical bonds, electronegativity, and how bond polarity arises. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIc-15.
objectives: Explain why atoms form chemical bonds and describe the octet rule
Distinguish between ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds
Define electronegativity and use it to predict bond polarity
Classify bonds as nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic based on electronegativity differences
Draw Lewis structures for simple molecules and ions

vocabulary.definition: A lasting attraction between atoms that enables the formation of chemical compounds.
The tendency of atoms to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve a full outer shell of eight electrons.
A bond formed by the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions — typically between a metal and a nonmetal.
A bond formed by the sharing of electron pairs between atoms — typically between nonmetals.
A bond in metals where valence electrons are delocalized and shared among a lattice of positive ions.
A measure of an atom's tendency to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond.
A covalent bond in which electrons are unequally shared due to an electronegativity difference between atoms.
A covalent bond in which electrons are shared equally because the atoms have similar electronegativities.

body:
🔗 Why Atoms Bond

Atoms bond to become more stable. Most atoms are most stable when their outermost electron shell is full — typically eight electrons, known as the octet rule. Noble gases (Group 18) already have full outer shells and rarely bond. Other elements gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve a noble gas configuration.

🧲 Types of Chemical Bonds

There are three main types of bonds:

  • Ionic bonds — Formed when one atom transfers electrons to another, creating positive and negative ions. Example: NaCl (sodium chloride). Metals lose electrons (become cations); nonmetals gain electrons (become anions).
  • Covalent bonds — Formed when atoms share electron pairs. Example: H₂O, CO₂, CH₄. Nonmetals share electrons to complete their octets.
  • Metallic bonds — Formed in metals where valence electrons are delocalized, creating a 'sea of electrons' that holds positive metal ions together. This explains why metals conduct electricity and heat.

⚡ Electronegativity: The Key to Polarity

Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract shared electrons. The Pauling scale ranges from 0.7 (francium) to 4.0 (fluorine). Key values:

  • F: 4.0 (most electronegative)
  • O: 3.5
  • N: 3.0
  • Cl: 3.0
  • C: 2.5
  • H: 2.1
  • Na: 0.9

The difference in electronegativity (ΔEN) between two bonded atoms determines bond type:

  • ΔEN < 0.4 → nonpolar covalent
  • 0.4 ≤ ΔEN < 1.7 → polar covalent
  • ΔEN ≥ 1.7 → ionic

🧪 Worked Example: Predicting Bond Type

Question: Classify the bonds in (a) H₂, (b) HCl, (c) NaCl.

Solution:

  • H₂: ΔEN = |2.1 - 2.1| = 0 → nonpolar covalent
  • HCl: ΔEN = |3.0 - 2.1| = 0.9 → polar covalent (Cl is more electronegative, so Cl is partially negative, H is partially positive)
  • NaCl: ΔEN = |3.0 - 0.9| = 2.1 → ionic

📝 Lewis Structures

Lewis structures show valence electrons as dots. Steps to draw them:

  • Count total valence electrons.
  • Place the least electronegative atom in the center.
  • Connect atoms with single bonds (2 electrons each).
  • Distribute remaining electrons to complete octets.
  • Form double or triple bonds if needed.

Example: H₂O — O in center, two H atoms bonded, two lone pairs on O.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Salt (NaCl) — Ionic bonding gives salt its high melting point and solubility in water.
  • Water (H₂O) — Polar covalent bonds make water a universal solvent.
  • Metals — Metallic bonding explains conductivity, malleability, and luster.
  • Diamond and graphite — Both made of carbon but different bonding arrangements give vastly different properties.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'All bonds are either purely ionic or purely covalent.' Reality: Bonding is a continuum. Most bonds have some ionic and some covalent character.
  • Misconception: 'Electronegativity is the same as electron affinity.' Reality: Electronegativity is the tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond; electron affinity is the energy change when an atom gains an electron.
  • Misconception: 'Lewis structures show the actual shape of molecules.' Reality: Lewis structures show connectivity and electron distribution, not 3D shape. VSEPR theory is needed for shape.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine three bonding scenarios. In ionic bonding, a sodium atom transfers an electron to a chlorine atom, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that attract each other. In covalent bonding, two hydrogen atoms share a pair of electrons. In metallic bonding, positive metal ions are surrounded by a sea of delocalized electrons.

2.intro: Once we know the bonds in a molecule, the next question is: what shape is it? The three-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule — its molecular geometry — determines its polarity, reactivity, and biological function. This lesson explores VSEPR theory, molecular shapes, and how geometry affects molecular polarity. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIc-16.

body:
📐 VSEPR Theory

VSEPR theory states that electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible. This minimizes repulsion and determines molecular shape.

Repulsion strength: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair. This means lone pairs push bonds closer together, reducing bond angles.

🔷 Common Molecular Geometries

Based on the number of electron domains (bonding + lone pairs) around the central atom:

  • 2 domains: Linear (180°) — e.g., CO₂
  • 3 domains: Trigonal planar (120°) — e.g., BF₃; Bent (~117°) if one lone pair — e.g., SO₂
  • 4 domains: Tetrahedral (109.5°) — e.g., CH₄; Trigonal pyramidal (~107°) if one lone pair — e.g., NH₃; Bent (~104.5°) if two lone pairs — e.g., H₂O
  • 5 domains: Trigonal bipyramidal (90°, 120°) — e.g., PCl₅
  • 6 domains: Octahedral (90°) — e.g., SF₆

🧪 Worked Example: Predicting Shape and Polarity

Question: Determine the shape and polarity of (a) CH₄, (b) NH₃, (c) H₂O.

Solution:

  • CH₄: 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs → tetrahedral. C-H bonds are weakly polar, but symmetry cancels dipoles → nonpolar molecule.
  • NH₃: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair → trigonal pyramidal. N-H bonds are polar, and the lone pair creates an asymmetric charge distribution → polar molecule.
  • H₂O: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs → bent. O-H bonds are polar, and the bent shape does not cancel dipoles → polar molecule.

⚖️ Symmetry and Polarity

A molecule is nonpolar if:

  • All bonds are nonpolar, OR
  • Polar bonds are arranged symmetrically so their dipoles cancel.

Examples of nonpolar molecules with polar bonds: CO₂ (linear, dipoles cancel), CCl₄ (tetrahedral, dipoles cancel), BF₃ (trigonal planar, dipoles cancel).

Examples of polar molecules: H₂O (bent), NH₃ (trigonal pyramidal), HCl (linear but asymmetric).

🌡️ How Geometry Affects Properties

Molecular shape and polarity determine:

  • Boiling point — Polar molecules have higher boiling points than nonpolar molecules of similar mass because of dipole-dipole attractions.
  • Solubility — 'Like dissolves like': polar solvents dissolve polar solutes; nonpolar solvents dissolve nonpolar solutes.
  • Biological activity — The shape of a molecule determines how it fits into enzyme active sites (lock-and-key model).

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Water — Bent shape and polarity make water an excellent solvent and give it a high boiling point.
  • Carbon dioxide — Linear and nonpolar, CO₂ is a gas at room temperature.
  • Ammonia — Trigonal pyramidal and polar, NH₃ is highly soluble in water.
  • Drug design — Molecular shape determines how drugs bind to receptors.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Molecules with polar bonds are always polar.' Reality: Symmetrical molecules with polar bonds (CO₂, CCl₄) are nonpolar because dipoles cancel.
  • Misconception: 'Lone pairs don't affect shape.' Reality: Lone pairs occupy space and push bonding pairs closer, reducing bond angles.
  • Misconception: 'Lewis structures show 3D shape.' Reality: Lewis structures show connectivity; VSEPR theory predicts 3D shape.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine four molecular shapes side by side. Linear CO₂: O=C=O with 180° bond angle. Trigonal planar BF₃: three F atoms around B at 120°. Tetrahedral CH₄: four H atoms around C at 109.5°. Bent H₂O: two H atoms around O at 104.5° with two lone pairs. Each shape affects how dipoles add or cancel.

3.intro: Even after understanding chemical bonds and molecular shape, there is another level of attraction that holds molecules together: intermolecular forces (IMFs). These forces are weaker than chemical bonds but determine whether a substance is a gas, liquid, or solid at room temperature. This lesson explores the three main types of IMFs — London dispersion, dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding — and how they affect physical properties. It aligns with competency code S11/12PS-IIIc-d-17.

body:
🔗 What Are Intermolecular Forces?

Intermolecular forces (IMFs) are the attractions between molecules. They are much weaker than chemical bonds (intramolecular forces) but determine whether a substance is a gas, liquid, or solid at a given temperature. Stronger IMFs → higher boiling point, melting point, viscosity, and surface tension.

🌊 London Dispersion Forces

London dispersion forces are the weakest IMFs and exist between all molecules. They arise from temporary fluctuations in electron distribution, creating instantaneous dipoles that induce dipoles in neighboring molecules. Dispersion forces increase with:

  • Molecular size — larger molecules have more electrons and are more polarizable.
  • Molecular shape — long, flat molecules have more surface contact and stronger dispersion forces.

Example: I₂ (solid) has stronger dispersion forces than Cl₂ (gas) because iodine is larger and more polarizable.

🧲 Dipole-Dipole Forces

Dipole-dipole forces occur between polar molecules. The positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of another. These forces are stronger than dispersion forces but weaker than hydrogen bonds.

Example: HCl molecules align so that the H (δ+) of one molecule faces the Cl (δ-) of another.

💧 Hydrogen Bonding

Hydrogen bonds are a special, strong type of dipole-dipole attraction. They occur when hydrogen is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O, or F) and interacts with a lone pair on another N, O, or F atom.

Hydrogen bonds are responsible for:

  • Water's high boiling point (100°C) compared to H₂S (-60°C)
  • Ice floating on water (hydrogen bonds form a hexagonal lattice that is less dense than liquid water)
  • DNA's double helix structure (base pairing via hydrogen bonds)
  • Protein secondary structure (alpha helices and beta sheets)

📊 Ranking IMF Strength

From weakest to strongest:

  • London dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding < ionic bonding < covalent bonding

Note: IMFs are much weaker than chemical bonds. Typical energies: IMFs ~0.1–40 kJ/mol; covalent bonds ~150–1000 kJ/mol.

🧮 Worked Example: Predicting Boiling Points

Question: Arrange the following in order of increasing boiling point: CH₄, CH₃OH, CH₃CH₃.

Solution:

  • CH₄ (methane): Nonpolar, only dispersion forces → lowest boiling point (-161°C).
  • CH₃CH₃ (ethane): Nonpolar, more electrons than CH₄ → stronger dispersion forces → boiling point -89°C.
  • CH₃OH (methanol): Polar, can form hydrogen bonds → highest boiling point (65°C).

Order: CH₄ < CH₃CH₃ < CH₃OH.

🌡️ How IMFs Affect Physical Properties

  • Boiling point — Stronger IMFs require more energy to overcome → higher boiling point.
  • Melting point — Stronger IMFs → higher melting point.
  • Viscosity — Stronger IMFs → more resistance to flow.
  • Surface tension — Stronger IMFs → higher surface tension.
  • Vapor pressure — Stronger IMFs → lower vapor pressure.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Water's high boiling point — Hydrogen bonding keeps water liquid at room temperature, essential for life.
  • DNA structure — Hydrogen bonds between base pairs hold the double helix together and allow replication.
  • Gecko adhesion — Geckos climb walls using dispersion forces between their toe pads and surfaces.
  • Lubricants — Weak IMFs allow oils to flow easily.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Intermolecular forces are the same as chemical bonds.' Reality: IMFs are much weaker and occur between molecules, not within them.
  • Misconception: 'Hydrogen bonds are actual bonds.' Reality: Hydrogen bonds are strong IMFs, not covalent bonds.
  • Misconception: 'All polar molecules have hydrogen bonds.' Reality: Hydrogen bonds require H bonded to N, O, or F. HCl is polar but does not form hydrogen bonds.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine three scenarios. In dispersion forces, two nonpolar molecules have temporary dipoles that attract each other. In dipole-dipole forces, two polar molecules align with positive and negative ends facing. In hydrogen bonding, water molecules form a network where each H of one molecule is attracted to the O of another, creating a strong, directional interaction.

4.intro: Intermolecular forces are not just abstract concepts — they govern the behavior of real substances, from the water we drink to the plastics we use. This lesson explores how IMFs explain the properties of liquids and solids, and how they are exploited in everyday products like soaps, detergents, and cosmetics. It aligns with competency codes S11/12PS-IIId-e-18, -19, and -20.
objectives: Explain how intermolecular forces determine the properties of liquids (vapor pressure, boiling point, viscosity, surface tension)
Describe the structure and properties of solids (crystalline vs. amorphous)
Explain how surfactants (soaps and detergents) work using IMF concepts

Predict how changes in molecular structure affect IMFs and physical properties

A solid with a regular, repeating arrangement of atoms or molecules (e.g., salt, diamond).
A solid with a random, disordered arrangement of atoms or molecules (e.g., glass, rubber).
A molecule with a hydrophilic (water-loving) head and a hydrophobic (water-fearing) tail — reduces surface tension and helps remove dirt.

Having an affinity for water — polar or ionic groups that interact with water via hydrogen bonding.
Having an aversion to water — nonpolar groups that do not interact with water.

body:
💧 Properties of Liquids and IMFs

The strength of IMFs determines liquid properties:

  • Vapor pressure — Weak IMFs → high vapor pressure (volatile liquids like gasoline). Strong IMFs → low vapor pressure (water, glycerol).
  • Boiling point — Strong IMFs → higher boiling point.
  • Viscosity — Strong IMFs → higher viscosity (honey vs. water).
  • Surface tension — Strong IMFs → higher surface tension (water beads up on wax).

🧊 Solids: Crystalline vs. Amorphous

Crystalline solids have a regular, repeating arrangement of particles. Examples: salt (NaCl), diamond, quartz. They have sharp melting points and well-defined shapes.

Amorphous solids have a random, disordered arrangement. Examples: glass, rubber, plastics. They soften over a range of temperatures rather than melting sharply.

🧼 How Soaps and Detergents Work

Soap molecules are surfactants — they have a hydrophilic (polar) head and a hydrophobic (nonpolar) tail. When soap is added to water:

  • The hydrophobic tails attach to oil and grease.
  • The hydrophilic heads face outward, interacting with water.
  • This forms micelles — spherical structures that trap oil inside and keep it suspended in water.
  • The oil is then rinsed away with water.

Detergents are synthetic surfactants that work similarly but are more effective in hard water (which contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions that react with soap to form scum).

💄 IMFs in Cosmetics

Cosmetics use IMF principles to achieve desired textures and effects:

  • Moisturizers — Humectants (glycerol, hyaluronic acid) form hydrogen bonds with water, drawing it into the skin.
  • Lipstick — Waxes and oils with strong IMFs provide structure and adherence.
  • Sunscreen — Active ingredients absorb UV radiation; emollients improve spreadability.
  • Nail polish — Solvents evaporate (weak IMFs), leaving a polymer film (strong IMFs).

🧪 Worked Example: Comparing Viscosity

Question: Explain why honey is more viscous than water.

Solution:

  • Honey is composed of sugars (glucose, fructose) with many -OH groups.
  • These -OH groups form extensive hydrogen bonds with each other.
  • Water also forms hydrogen bonds, but honey molecules are larger and have more hydrogen-bonding sites.
  • More hydrogen bonds → stronger IMFs → higher viscosity.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Hard water — Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions interfere with soap, reducing cleaning efficiency. Detergents solve this problem.
  • Emulsions — Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil in water stabilized by lecithin (from egg yolk).
  • Waterproofing — Hydrophobic coatings (e.g., on rain jackets) repel water by minimizing IMFs with water.
  • Drug delivery — Liposomes (micelle-like structures) encapsulate drugs for targeted delivery.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Soap kills bacteria.' Reality: Soap removes bacteria by trapping them in micelles and rinsing them away. Some soaps contain antibacterial agents, but plain soap is effective through physical removal.
  • Misconception: 'All liquids with strong IMFs are viscous.' Reality: Viscosity also depends on molecular shape and temperature. Strong IMFs generally increase viscosity, but shape matters too.
  • Misconception: 'Glass is a liquid.' Reality: Glass is an amorphous solid. It does not flow at room temperature on human timescales.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a micelle in water. The outer surface is made of hydrophilic heads (circles) facing the water. The inner core contains hydrophobic tails (wavy lines) and trapped oil droplets. This structure allows oil to be suspended in water and rinsed away.

1.intro: Chemical reactions are the heart of industrial chemistry — from manufacturing fertilizers to producing plastics. But not all reactions are equally fast or efficient. Some occur in seconds; others take years. This lesson explores chemical kinetics: the factors that affect reaction rates and how we can control them to optimize industrial processes. It aligns with competency codes S11/12PS-IIId-e-21 and IIId-e-24.

Describe the collision theory of chemical reactions

vocabulary.definition: The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time — usually expressed in mol/L·s.
The theory that chemical reactions occur when particles collide with sufficient energy and proper orientation.
The minimum energy required for a collision to result in a chemical reaction.
A substance that increases reaction rate by lowering activation energy without being consumed in the reaction.
A catalyst in the same phase as the reactants — e.g., an aqueous acid catalyst in a liquid reaction.
A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants — e.g., a solid metal catalyst with gaseous reactants.

body:
⚡ What Is Reaction Rate?

Reaction rate is the speed at which reactants are converted into products. It is measured by tracking the decrease in reactant concentration or the increase in product concentration over time. For example, the rate of rusting (iron + oxygen → iron oxide) is very slow, while the rate of combustion (methane + oxygen → CO₂ + H₂O) is very fast.

Rate = Δ[concentration] / Δtime

🎯 Collision Theory

Collision theory states that for a reaction to occur, particles must:

  • Collide — particles must physically meet.
  • Have sufficient energy — the collision energy must exceed the activation energy (Ea).
  • Have proper orientation — the reacting parts of the molecules must be aligned correctly.

Not all collisions lead to reactions. Only effective collisions — those meeting all three criteria — result in product formation.

🌡️ Factors Affecting Reaction Rate

1. Concentration — Higher concentration means more particles in a given volume, leading to more frequent collisions and faster reactions.

2. Temperature — Higher temperature increases particle kinetic energy, so more collisions exceed the activation energy. A general rule: reaction rate doubles for every 10°C increase.

3. Surface Area — For solid reactants, smaller particles have greater surface area, allowing more collisions. Powdered sugar dissolves faster than a sugar cube.

4. Catalysts — Catalysts lower activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway. They are not consumed in the reaction.

5. Pressure — For gaseous reactions, increasing pressure increases concentration, leading to more collisions.

🧪 How Catalysts Work

Catalysts speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy barrier. They do this by:

  • Providing a surface for reactants to align (heterogeneous catalysts).
  • Forming temporary intermediate compounds that react more easily (homogeneous catalysts).
  • Weakening bonds in reactant molecules, making them easier to break.

Examples: Iron in the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃), platinum in catalytic converters (converts CO and NOx to CO₂ and N₂), enzymes in biological systems.

🧮 Worked Example: Calculating Reaction Rate

Question: In a reaction A → B, the concentration of A decreases from 0.80 M to 0.20 M in 60 seconds. Calculate the average reaction rate.

Solution:

  • Δ[A] = 0.20 M - 0.80 M = -0.60 M
  • Δt = 60 s
  • Rate = -Δ[A] / Δt = -(-0.60 M) / 60 s = 0.010 M/s

The average rate is 0.010 mol/L·s.

🏭 The Haber Process: A Case Study

The Haber process synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen:

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat

Conditions: 400–500°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst. These conditions balance rate (higher temperature speeds reaction) with yield (lower temperature favors product, but is too slow without catalyst).

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Food preservation — Refrigeration slows bacterial reactions; canning uses heat to speed sterilization.
  • Catalytic converters — Reduce vehicle emissions by converting harmful gases to less harmful ones.
  • Enzymes — Biological catalysts that speed up digestion and metabolism.
  • Fertilizer production — The Haber process produces ammonia for fertilizers, feeding billions.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Catalysts are consumed in reactions.' Reality: Catalysts are not consumed; they can be recovered unchanged.
  • Misconception: 'Higher temperature always means faster reaction.' Reality: Higher temperature speeds reactions but can also decompose products or favor reverse reactions in reversible processes.
  • Misconception: 'Reactions stop when reactants are gone.' Reality: Reactions stop when the limiting reactant is consumed or equilibrium is reached.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine an energy diagram with reactants on the left and products on the right. The curve rises to a peak representing activation energy. A catalyst lowers this peak, allowing more collisions to result in reaction. The energy difference between reactants and products (ΔH) remains unchanged.

The calculation of quantities of reactants and products in a chemical reaction.

body:
⚖️ The Mole: Chemistry's Counting Unit

A mole (mol) is the amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules, ions). This number — Avogadro's number — allows chemists to count particles by weighing them. One mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to its atomic or molecular mass.

Example: 1 mol of H₂O = 18.02 g = 6.022 × 10²³ water molecules.

🔄 Conversions Between Mass, Moles, and Particles

Key conversion factors:

  • Mass → moles: n = m / M (where M is molar mass)
  • Moles → particles: N = n × 6.022 × 10²³
  • Moles → volume (gas at STP): V = n × 22.4 L

🧮 Worked Example: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry

Question: How many grams of water are produced when 32 g of methane (CH₄) burns completely in oxygen?

Equation: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

Solution:

  • Molar mass of CH₄ = 12.01 + 4(1.008) = 16.04 g/mol
  • Moles of CH₄ = 32 g / 16.04 g/mol = 2.00 mol
  • From equation: 1 mol CH₄ → 2 mol H₂O
  • Moles of H₂O = 2.00 × 2 = 4.00 mol
  • Molar mass of H₂O = 18.02 g/mol
  • Mass of H₂O = 4.00 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 72.1 g

🎯 Limiting Reactant

The limiting reactant is the reactant that is completely consumed first, limiting the amount of product. To identify it:

  • Calculate moles of each reactant.
  • Divide moles by the stoichiometric coefficient.
  • The smallest result is the limiting reactant.

Example: If you have 4 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ for the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, H₂ is in excess and O₂ is limiting (1 mol O₂ requires 2 mol H₂; you have 4, so O₂ limits).

📊 Percent Yield

Theoretical yield is the maximum product calculated from stoichiometry. Actual yield is the amount actually obtained. Percent yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100%.

Actual yield is often less than theoretical because of:

  • Side reactions
  • Incomplete reactions
  • Loss during transfer and purification
  • Impurities in reactants

🧪 Worked Example: Limiting Reactant and Percent Yield

Question: 10.0 g of N₂ reacts with 10.0 g of H₂ to form NH₃. If 8.0 g of NH₃ is obtained, what is the percent yield?

Equation: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃

Solution:

  • Moles N₂ = 10.0 / 28.02 = 0.357 mol
  • Moles H₂ = 10.0 / 2.02 = 4.95 mol
  • Divide by coefficients: N₂: 0.357/1 = 0.357; H₂: 4.95/3 = 1.65
  • N₂ is limiting.
  • Theoretical NH₃ = 0.357 × 2 = 0.714 mol × 17.03 g/mol = 12.2 g
  • Percent yield = (8.0 / 12.2) × 100% = 65.6%

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Pharmaceuticals — Stoichiometry ensures correct drug doses.
  • Agriculture — Fertilizer amounts are calculated to maximize crop yield.
  • Manufacturing — Limiting reactants determine cost-effectiveness.
  • Environmental science — Stoichiometry predicts pollutant formation in combustion.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'The limiting reactant is the one with the smallest mass.' Reality: It depends on molar amounts and stoichiometric coefficients, not just mass.
  • Misconception: 'Percent yield can be over 100%.' Reality: Percent yield >100% indicates impurities or measurement errors, not extra product.
  • Misconception: 'Moles and molecules are the same.' Reality: A mole is a counting unit (like a dozen); molecules are the actual particles.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a recipe analogy: to make a sandwich, you need 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. If you have 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese, cheese is the limiting reactant — you can make only 3 sandwiches, and 4 slices of bread remain. Stoichiometry works the same way.

3.intro: Every chemical reaction involves energy changes — some release energy (exothermic), and some absorb energy (endothermic). Understanding these energy changes is crucial for industrial chemistry, where energy efficiency determines profitability and environmental impact. This lesson explores thermochemistry: enthalpy, calorimetry, and Hess's law. It aligns with competency codes S11/12PS-IIId-h-25 and IIId-h-26.
objectives: Distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions
Define enthalpy (ΔH) and explain how it relates to heat flow
Use calorimetry to measure heat changes in chemical reactions

Explain the importance of energy changes in industrial processes

vocabulary.definition: The study of energy changes that accompany chemical reactions and physical changes.
A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings — ΔH is negative.
A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings — ΔH is positive.
The total heat content of a system at constant pressure — ΔH is the change in enthalpy.
The measurement of heat changes in chemical reactions using a calorimeter.
The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1°C.
The total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the pathway — it depends only on initial and final states.
The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states.

body:
🔥 Exothermic vs. Endothermic

Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings. Examples: combustion, respiration, neutralization. The products have lower enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is negative.

Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings. Examples: photosynthesis, melting ice, thermal decomposition. The products have higher enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH is positive.

📊 Enthalpy Diagrams

In an exothermic reaction, the products are lower in energy than the reactants — the difference is released as heat. In an endothermic reaction, the products are higher in energy — heat is absorbed from the surroundings.

ΔH = H(products) - H(reactants)

🧪 Calorimetry: Measuring Heat

Calorimetry measures heat changes using a calorimeter. The heat released or absorbed is calculated using:

q = m × c × ΔT

where q = heat (J), m = mass (g), c = specific heat capacity (J/g·°C), ΔT = temperature change (°C).

For water, c = 4.18 J/g·°C. In a coffee-cup calorimeter, the heat released by a reaction is absorbed by the water, and q(reaction) = -q(water).

🧮 Worked Example: Calorimetry Calculation

Question: When 50.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl reacts with 50.0 mL of 1.0 M NaOH in a coffee-cup calorimeter, the temperature rises from 25.0°C to 31.5°C. Calculate the heat released (assume density = 1.0 g/mL, c = 4.18 J/g·°C).

Solution:

  • Total mass = 50.0 + 50.0 = 100.0 g
  • ΔT = 31.5 - 25.0 = 6.5°C
  • q = m × c × ΔT = 100.0 × 4.18 × 6.5 = 2,717 J = 2.72 kJ
  • q(reaction) = -2.72 kJ (exothermic, heat released)

⚖️ Hess's Law

Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or multiple steps. This allows us to calculate ΔH for reactions that are difficult to measure directly.

Example: To find ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO, we can use:

  • C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH₁ = -393.5 kJ
  • CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH₂ = -283.0 kJ
  • Reverse second: CO₂ → CO + ½O₂, ΔH = +283.0 kJ
  • Add: C + O₂ → CO₂ + CO₂ → CO + ½O₂ = C + ½O₂ → CO
  • ΔH = -393.5 + 283.0 = -110.5 kJ

🏭 Energy in Industry

Energy changes determine:

  • Feasibility — Endothermic reactions require energy input, increasing costs.
  • Safety — Exothermic reactions can cause runaway heating and explosions.
  • Efficiency — Heat recovery systems capture exothermic heat to drive endothermic steps.
  • Environmental impact — Energy consumption contributes to carbon emissions.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Hand warmers — Use exothermic crystallization of sodium acetate.
  • Cold packs — Use endothermic dissolution of ammonium nitrate.
  • Combustion engines — Convert chemical energy to heat and mechanical work.
  • Photosynthesis — Endothermic process storing solar energy in glucose.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Exothermic reactions are always spontaneous.' Reality: Spontaneity depends on both enthalpy and entropy (Gibbs free energy).
  • Misconception: 'Endothermic reactions cannot occur.' Reality: They can occur if enough energy is supplied.
  • Misconception: 'ΔH is the same as activation energy.' Reality: ΔH is the enthalpy change between reactants and products; activation energy is the barrier to reaction.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine two energy diagrams. In the exothermic diagram, reactants are higher than products, with ΔH negative. In the endothermic diagram, reactants are lower than products, with ΔH positive. Both diagrams show an activation energy peak, which a catalyst can lower.

4.intro: Industrial chemistry is not just about reactions in test tubes — it is about scaling up those reactions to produce tons of material safely, efficiently, and economically. This lesson explores the principles of industrial chemistry, including process design, green chemistry, and the production of key chemicals like ammonia, sulfuric acid, and plastics. It aligns with competency codes S11/12PS-IIIh-27, IIIi-28, and IIIi-29.
objectives: Describe the key considerations in designing an industrial chemical process
Explain the Haber process and the Contact process for producing ammonia and sulfuric acid
Describe the production of common polymers (plastics) and their environmental impact
Apply the principles of green chemistry to evaluate industrial processes
Discuss the role of catalysis, energy efficiency, and waste reduction in sustainable industry

vocabulary.definition: The branch of chemistry concerned with the large-scale production of chemicals for commercial use.
The industrial synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst at high temperature and pressure.
The industrial production of sulfuric acid by oxidizing sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide using a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.
A large molecule made of repeating subunits (monomers) — e.g., polyethylene, polystyrene.
A small molecule that can bond with others to form a polymer.
The design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and waste.
The efficiency of a reaction in incorporating reactant atoms into the final product — higher is better.

body:
🏭 Principles of Industrial Chemistry

Industrial chemical processes must balance:

  • Yield — Maximize product formation.
  • Rate — Produce quickly enough to meet demand.
  • Cost — Minimize energy, raw materials, and labor.
  • Safety — Prevent accidents and protect workers.
  • Environmental impact — Reduce waste and emissions.

These factors often conflict — e.g., high temperature increases rate but may decrease yield for exothermic reactions.

🧪 The Haber Process

The Haber process produces ammonia for fertilizers:

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat

Conditions: 400–500°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst with potassium and aluminum oxide promoters.

Why these conditions?

  • High pressure favors the product (fewer gas molecules).
  • Moderate temperature balances rate and yield.
  • Catalyst speeds the reaction without being consumed.
  • Ammonia is removed continuously to shift equilibrium right.

🧪 The Contact Process

The Contact process produces sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), the most produced industrial chemical:

  • S + O₂ → SO₂ (burning sulfur)
  • 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, 400–450°C, 1–2 atm)
  • SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum)
  • H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄

Sulfuric acid is used in fertilizers, batteries, and chemical synthesis.

🧴 Polymers and Plastics

Polymers are large molecules made of repeating monomers. Examples:

  • Polyethylene — from ethylene (C₂H₄), used in bags and bottles.
  • Polypropylene — from propylene, used in containers and textiles.
  • Polystyrene — from styrene, used in foam and packaging.
  • PVC — from vinyl chloride, used in pipes and cables.

Plastics are durable and versatile but persist in the environment for centuries, contributing to pollution.

🌱 Green Chemistry

Green chemistry aims to reduce hazardous substances and waste. Key principles:

  • Prevent waste — Design processes that minimize byproducts.
  • Atom economy — Maximize incorporation of reactants into products.
  • Safer solvents — Use water or supercritical CO₂ instead of toxic organic solvents.
  • Energy efficiency — Run reactions at ambient temperature and pressure when possible.
  • Renewable feedstocks — Use biomass instead of fossil fuels.

🧮 Worked Example: Atom Economy

Question: Calculate the atom economy for the reaction: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH (ethanol).

Solution:

  • Molar mass of reactants: C₂H₄ (28.05) + H₂O (18.02) = 46.07 g/mol
  • Molar mass of product: C₂H₅OH = 46.07 g/mol
  • Atom economy = (46.07 / 46.07) × 100% = 100%

This reaction has perfect atom economy — all reactant atoms end up in the product.

🌍 Real-World Connections

  • Fertilizers — Haber process ammonia feeds billions.
  • Batteries — Sulfuric acid is the electrolyte in lead-acid batteries.
  • Plastics recycling — Mechanical and chemical recycling reduce plastic waste.
  • Pharmaceuticals — Green chemistry reduces waste and cost in drug synthesis.

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

  • Misconception: 'Industrial chemistry is just scaled-up lab chemistry.' Reality: Scaling up introduces challenges in heat transfer, mixing, and safety.
  • Misconception: 'Catalysts last forever.' Reality: Catalysts can be poisoned by impurities and must be regenerated or replaced.
  • Misconception: 'Green chemistry is more expensive.' Reality: It often reduces costs by minimizing waste and energy use.

📊 Diagram Description

Imagine a flowchart of the Haber process: nitrogen and hydrogen gases enter a compressor, then pass through a catalyst bed at high temperature and pressure. Ammonia is condensed and removed, while unreacted gases are recycled. This continuous loop maximizes efficiency.

1.intro: Every time you wash your hands, brush your teeth, or apply lotion, you are using products of consumer chemistry. These products are carefully formulated using chemical principles to clean, protect, and improve our daily lives. This lesson explores the chemistry of cleaning agents — soaps, detergents, and disinfectants — and how they work at the molecular level. It aligns with competency codes S11/12PS-IIIi-j-30, -31, -32.
objectives: Describe the structure and function of soaps and detergents as surfactants

Explain the concept of pH and how it relates to cleaning product effectiveness
